paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Imagine two drivers who each, for a moment, take their eyes off the road to read a message. One is lucky: nothing is in her path, and she looks up in time. The other is unlucky: a child steps out, and he cannot stop. Most people believe that the second driver is far more blameworthy than the first, and that he deserves punishment while she does not. Yet the two did exactly the same thing. The philosopher Thomas Nagel called such cases moral luck, and he saw in them a challenge to one of our deepest assumptions: that we are responsible only for what is within our control.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The puzzle arises because the principle of control seems compelling. It would be unfair, we feel, to blame someone for something they could not have prevented. Yet our everyday practice does not follow the principle. We judge the unlucky driver harshly, and the law reflects this: a person who attempts to murder and fails is typically punished less severely than one who succeeds, although the difference lies only in circumstances beyond their control. Philosophers have identified several kinds of moral luck, including luck in outcomes, luck in circumstances, such as living in a time when cruelty was demanded or tolerated, and even luck in character, since nobody chooses their upbringing.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One response is to deny that the cases are as they appear. According to this view, the drivers do deserve equal blame, and our reaction to the second is an emotional response which should not guide a reasoned judgement. Some legal systems approach this position in principle, although few apply it consistently. The difficulty is that it seems to ask us to stop reacting as humans do. Many people feel that a wrongdoer who causes terrible harm has done something worse than one who narrowly avoided it, and that a theory which cannot accommodate this has missed something.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second response accepts the intuition and abandons the control principle, at least in part. We are responsible, it argues, not merely for our choices but for the person we turn out to be, including the consequences that follow. This fits the way we feel about apologies: the unlucky driver ought to feel profound regret, even though he was no more careless than anyone else. A person who shrugged and said, it was just bad luck, would seem to have failed morally. The price of this approach is that responsibility becomes less tidy, for it extends to what we cannot fully control.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Neither response is entirely satisfactory, which is why the debate has endured for decades. What the puzzle reveals, I believe, is that our moral concepts are not the clean instruments that philosophers would like. They emerge from a human life in which we act without foresight, are affected by chance, and are nevertheless held to account. To recognise this does not require us to abandon moral judgement, but it does recommend a degree of humility, towards those we blame and towards ourselves.
